questiontext.text: When an LRU cache is full and a new key must be inserted, which item does it evict?

answer.text: The least recently used item

feedback.text: Correct — LRU evicts the entry whose last access is oldest.

answer.text: The most recently used item

feedback.text: That is the opposite; the most recent item is the one you want to keep.

answer.text: A uniformly random item

feedback.text: That is random replacement, not LRU.

answer.text: The item with the largest key

feedback.text: LRU orders by recency of access, not by key value.

generalfeedback.text: LRU stands for Least Recently Used: when at capacity it discards the entry that has gone the longest without being accessed.

questiontext.text: Which pair of structures gives an LRU cache O(1) get and put?

answer.text: A hash map (key → node) plus a doubly linked list

feedback.text: Correct — the map gives O(1) lookup; the list gives O(1) reordering and eviction.

answer.text: A single sorted array

feedback.text: Keeping it ordered by recency would cost O(n) per access.

answer.text: A binary heap keyed by timestamp

feedback.text: A heap gives O(log n) updates, not O(1).

answer.text: A singly linked list only

feedback.text: A singly linked list cannot unlink an interior node in O(1); you need a doubly linked list plus a map.

generalfeedback.text: The standard design pairs a hash map from key to list node with a doubly linked list that orders nodes by recency, giving O(1) get and put.

questiontext.text: Using the head-is-most-recent convention, what happens to a node on every successful get or put?

answer.text: It is moved to the head of the doubly linked list

feedback.text: Correct — touching a node marks it most-recently-used by moving it to the head.

answer.text: It is moved to the tail of the list

feedback.text: The tail is the least-recently-used end, reserved for eviction.

answer.text: It is deleted and reinserted at a random position

feedback.text: LRU maintains strict recency order, not random placement.

answer.text: Nothing — the list order never changes on access

feedback.text: Every access must update recency, or eviction would be wrong.

generalfeedback.text: Each access relinks the node to the head (most-recently-used); the least-recently-used node therefore drifts to the tail and is evicted first.

questiontext.text: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?

answer.text: Prev and next pointers let any interior node be unlinked in O(1)

feedback.text: Correct — with both links you splice a node out without walking the list.

answer.text: It halves the memory used per node

feedback.text: A doubly linked list uses more memory per node, not less.

answer.text: It keeps the entries sorted by key automatically

feedback.text: The list orders by recency, not by key, and does so manually.

answer.text: It removes the need for the hash map

feedback.text: The map is still required for O(1) key lookup.

generalfeedback.text: Moving a touched node to the head means removing it from its current position; only a doubly linked list can unlink an interior node in O(1) without a prior-node search.

questiontext.text: An LRU cache has a fixed capacity, and once it is full every new key forces an eviction.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the capacity is bounded, so inserting into a full cache evicts one entry.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A cache is capacity-bounded by definition; a full cache must evict to make room.

questiontext.text: With the hash map plus doubly linked list design, a get that also updates recency runs in O(log n) time.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: The map lookup and the list relinking are both O(1), so get is O(1), not O(log n).

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — get is O(1): O(1) map lookup plus O(1) move-to-head.

questiontext.text: With most-recently-used at the head, the least-recently-used node sits at the ______ of the doubly linked list, where eviction happens.

answer.text: tail

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: tail*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about an LRU cache are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: A hash map gives O(1) lookup from key to its list node

feedback.text: Yes — the map is what makes get constant time.

answer.text: A doubly linked list lets a node be unlinked and moved to the head in O(1)

feedback.text: Yes — two-way links allow O(1) removal of an interior node.

answer.text: It evicts the most recently used item when full

feedback.text: No — it evicts the least recently used item.

answer.text: It has unbounded capacity and never evicts

feedback.text: No — a cache has a fixed capacity and evicts when full.

generalfeedback.text: An LRU cache uses a hash map (O(1) lookup) and a doubly linked list (O(1) relink), has fixed capacity, and evicts the least recently used item.
